Or cobwebs, or Oates;
But helpe to ſcoure ye.
This is no Gowrie,
Has drawne James hither,
But the goodman of Bever,
Our Buckinghams Father;
Then ſo much the rather
Make it a jolly night,
For tis a holy night,
Spight of the Conſtable,
Or Mas Deane of Dunſtable.

sp.speaker: ALL.
sp.l: A Hall, a hall, a hall.

sp.speaker: PATRICO.
sp.l: WHy now ye behold,
Twas truth that I told,
And no deviſe;
They are chang'd in a trice,
And ſo will I,
Be my ſelfe, by and by.
I onely now
Muſt ſtudie now
To come off with a grace,
With my Patrico's place:
Some ſhort kind of bleſſing,
It ſelfe addreſſing
Unto my good Maſter,
Which light on him faſter,
Then wiſhes can flye.
And you that ſtand by
Be as jocund as I;
Each man with his voyce,
Give his heart to rejoyce,
Which I'le requite,
If my Art hit right,
Though late now at night,
Each Clowne here in ſight,
Before day light,
Shall prove a good Knight;
And your Laſſes Pages
Worthie their wages,
Where fancie engages
Girles to their ages.

sp.speaker: CLOVV.
sp.l: Oh any thing for the Patrico, what iſt? what iſt?

sp.speaker: PAT.
sp.l: Nothing, but beare the bob of the cloſe,
It will be no bruthen you well may ſuppoſe.
But bleſſe the Sov'raine, and his ſences,
An to wiſh away offences,

sp.speaker: CLO.
sp.l: Let us alone, bleſſe the Sov'raine, and his ſences.

sp.speaker: PAT.
sp.l: Wee'll take them in order, as they have being,
And firſt of ſeeing.

lg.l: FRom a Gipſie, in the morning,
Or a paire of ſquint-eyes turning:
From the Coblin, and the ſpectre,
Or a Drunkard, though with Nectar;
From a woman true to no man,
Which is ougly, beſides common;
A ſmocke rampant, and the itches,
To be putting on the breeches:
Wher ſo 'ere they ha' their being,
Bleſſe the Sov'raine, and his ſeeing.
From a Lawyer, three parts noyſe;
From impertinence, like a Drum
Beate at dinner in his roome;
From a tongue without a file,
Heapes of Phraſes, and no ſtile.
From a Fiddle out of tune,
As the Cuckow is in June.
From the candleſticks of Lothbury,
And the lowd pure wives of Banbury:
Or a long pretended fit;
Meant for mirth, but is not it:
Onely time, and eares out-wearing,
Bleſſe the Sov'raine, and his hearing.
FRom a ſtrolling Tinkers ſheete,
Or a payre of Carriers feet:
From a Ladie that doth breath,
Worſe above, then underneath.
From the Diet, and the knowledge
Of the ſtudents in Beares-colledge.
From Tobacco, with the tipe
Of the Devills gliſter-pipe;
Or a ſtincke all ſtincks excelling,
A Fiſhmongers dwelling,
Bleſſe the Sov'raigne, and his ſmelling.
FRom an Oyſter, and fry'd fiſh
A Sowes babye in a diſh:
From any portion of a Swine,
From bad Veniſon, and worſe wine.
Ling, what Cooke ſo'ere it boyle,
Though with muſtard fawc'd and oyle,
Or what elſe would keepe man faſting,
Bleſſe the Sov'raigne, and his taſting.
BOth from birdlime, and from pitch,
From a Doxie, and her itch.
From the briſles of a Hogge,
Or the ring-worme in a Dogge.
From the courtſhippe of a brier,
Or St. Anthonies old fier.
From a needle, or a thorne;
I'the bed at Ev'n, or Morne.
Or from any Gowtes leaſt grutching.
Bleſſe the Sov'raigne, and his touching.
BLeſſe him too from all offences,
In his ſports, as in his fences.
From a Boy to croſſe his way,
From a fall, or a foule day.
BLeſſe him, ô bleſſe him Heav'n, and lend him long
to be the ſacred burthen of all ſong;
The Acts, and yeares, of all our Kings t' out go;
And while hee's mortall, we not thinke him ſo.

div.stage: After which, aſcending up, the Jackman ſings.

div.head: SONG I.
div.l: THe ſports are done, yet doe not let
Your joyes in ſudden ſilence ſett;
Delight, and dumbneſſe never met
In one ſelfe ſubject yet.
If things oppos'd muſt mixt appeare,
Then adde a boldneſſe to your feare,
And ſpeake a hymne to him,
Where all your duties do of right belong,
Which I will ſweeten with an under ſong.

sp.speaker: CAPTAINE.
sp.l: GLory of ours, and grace of all the Eath;
How well your figure doth become your birth,
As if your forme, and fortune equall ſtood,
And onely vertue got above your blood.

div.head: SONG 2.
div.l: Vertue; his Kingly vertue which did merrit
This Iſle entire, and you are to inherit.

sp.speaker: 4 GIPSIE.
sp.l: HOw right he doth confeſſe him in his face,
His browe, his eye, and ev'ry marke of State;
As if he were the iſſue of each Grace,
And bore about him both his fame, and fate.

div.head: SONG 3.
div.l: LOoke, looke, is hee not faire,
And freſh, fragrant too
As Summer skie, or purged Aire,
And lookes as Lillies doe,
That were this morning blowne.

sp.speaker: 4 GIPSIE.
sp.l: Oh more! that more of him were knowne.

sp.speaker: 3 GIPSIE.
sp.l: LOoke how the Windes upon the Waves growne tame,
Take up Land ſounds upon their purple wings;
And catching each from other, beare the fame
To ev'ry angle of their ſacred ſprings.
So will we take his praiſe, and hurle his name
About the Globe, in thouſand Ay'ry rings,
If his great vertue be in lore with fame,
For that contem'd, both are neglected things.

div.head: SONG 4.
div.l: GOod Princes ſoare above their fame,
And in their worth,
Come greater forth,
Then in their name.
Such, ſuch the Father is,
Whom ev'ry title ſtrives to kiſſe;
Who on his Royall grounds unto himſelfe doth raiſe,
The worke to trouble fame, and to aſtoniſh praiſe.

sp.speaker: 4 GIPSIE.
sp.l: INdeed hee's not Lord alone of all the State,
But of the love of men, and of the Empires fate.
The Muſes Arts, the Schooles commerce, our honours lawes,
And Vertues hang on him, as on their working cauſe.

sp.speaker: 2 GIP.
sp.l: His Hand-mayd Juſtice is,

sp.speaker: 3 GIP.
sp.l: Wiſedome, his Wife;

sp.speaker: 4 GIP.
sp.l: His Miſtreſſe, Mercie;

sp.speaker: 5 GIP.
sp.l: Temperance, his life.

sp.speaker: 2 GIP.
sp.l: His Pages bounty, and grace which many prove,

sp.speaker: 3 GIP.
sp.l: His Guards are Magnanimitie, and love.

sp.speaker: 4 GIP.
sp.l: His Uſhers, Councell, Truth, and Pietie,

sp.speaker: 5 GIP.
sp.l: And all that followes him, Felicitie.

div.head: SONG 5.
div.l: OH that we underſtood
Our good;
Ther's happineſſe indeed in blood,
And ſtore,
But how much more,
When vertu's flood
In the ſame ſtreame doth hit?
As that growes high with yeares, ſo happineſſe with it.

sp.speaker: CAPTAINE.
sp.l: LOve, love his fortune then, and vertues knowne,
Who is the toppe of men,
But makes the happineſſe our owne;
Since where the Prince, for goodneſſe is renownd,
The Subject with Felicitie is Crownd.

div.head: The EPILOGUE.
div.l: AT Burley, Bever, and now laſt at Windſor,
Which ſhewes we are Gipſies of no common kinde Sir.
You have behold (and with delight) their change,
And how they came transform'd, may thinke it ſtrange.
It being a thing not touch't at by our Poet,
Good Ben ſlept there, or elſe forgot to ſhew it;
But leaſt it prove like wonder to the ſight,
To ſee a Gipſie, as an Aethiope, white.
Know, that what dy'd our faces, was an oyntment
Made, and layd on by Mr. Woolfes appointment,
The Court Licanthropos; yet without ſpells,
By a meere Barber, and no Magicke ells:
It was fetcht off with water, and a ball,
And to our transformation, this is all,
Save what the Maſter Faſhioner calls his,
For to Gipſies Metamorphoſis;
Who doth diſguiſe his habit, and his face,
And takes on a falſe perſon by his place:
The power of Poetrie can never faile her;
Aſſiſted by a Barber, and a Taylor.

div.head: THE MASQUE OF AUGURES. WITH THE SEVERALL ANTIMASQVES PRESENTED ON TWELFE-NIGHT, 1622.
The firſt Antimaſque had for the SCENE The Court Buttry-hatch.
div.stage: The Preſenters were from St. KATHARINES,
Notch a Brewers Clarke, Slug a Lighterman, Van-gooſe a rare Artiſt; Lady Alewife, her two Women, three dancing Beares, Urſon the Bear-ward, Groome of the Revells.

sp.speaker: NOTCH.
sp.p: COme, now my head's in, Ile even venture the whole: I ha ſeene the Lyons ere now, and he that hath ſeene them may ſee the King.

sp.speaker: SIVG.
sp.p: I think he may; but have a care you go not too high (neighbour Notch) leaſt you chance to have a Tally made of your pate, and bee clawed with a cudgell; there is as much danger going too neere the King, as the Lyons.

sp.speaker: GROOM.
sp.p: Whither? whither now gameſters? what is the buſineſſe? the affaire? ſtop I beſeech you.

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p: This muſt be an Officer, or nothing, he is ſo peart and breife in his demands! a pretty man! and a pretty man is a little o'this ſide nothing; howſoever we muſt not be daunted now, I am ſure I am a greater man than he out of the Court, and I have loſt nothing of my Sire ſince I came to it.

sp.speaker: GROOM.
sp.p: Hey-da! what's this? A hogſhead of beere broake out of the Kings buttery, ro ſome Dutch Hulke! whether are you bound? The winde is againſt you, you muſt backe; doe you know where you are?

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p:
Yes ſir, if we bee not miſtaken, we are at the Court, and would
be glad to ſpeake with ſomething of leſſe authority, and more wit, that knowes a little in the place.

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: Sir, I know as little as any man in the place; ſpeake, what is your buſineſſe? I am an Officer, Groome of the Revels, that is my place.

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p: To fetch Bonge of Court a parcell of inviſible bread, and beere for the Plaiers (for they never ſee it) or to miſtake ſixe Torches from the Chandry, and give them one.

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: How ſir?

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p: Come, this is not the firſt time you have carried coales to your owne houſe, I meane that ſhould have warm'd them.

sp.speaker: GROOM.
sp.p: Sir, I may doe it by my place, and I muſt queſtion you farther.

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p: Be not ſo muſty ſir, our deſire is only to know whether the Kings Majeſty, and the Court expect any diſguiſe here to night.

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: Diſguiſe! what meane you by that? doe you thinke that his Majeſty ſits here to expect drunkards?

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p: No, if hee did, I beleeve you would ſupply that place better then you do this: Diſguiſe was the old Engliſh word for a Maſque ſir, before you were an implement belonging to the Revels.

sp.speaker: GR.
sp.p: There is no ſuch word in the Office now I aſſure you ſir, I have ſerv'd here, man, and boy a Prentiſhip or twaine, and I ſhould know. But, by what name ſo ever you call it, here will be a Maſque, and ſhall be a Maſque, when you and the reſt of your Comrogues ſhall ſit diſguiſ'd in the ſtocks.

sp.speaker: NOTCH.
sp.p:
Sure by your language you were never meant for a Cour
• ier, howſoever it hath beene your ill fortune to be taken out of the neſt young; you are ſome Conſtables egge, ſome ſuch Widgin of Authoritie, you are ſo eaſily offended! Our comming was to ſhew our loves ſir, and to make a little merry with his Majeſty to night, and we have brought a Maſque with us, if his Majeſtie had not beene better provided.

sp.speaker: GROOME.
sp.p: Who you? you a Maſque? why you ſtincke like ſo many bloat-herrings newly taken out of the chimney! In the name of Ignorance, whence came you? or what are you? you have beene hang'd in the ſmoake ſufficiently, that is ſmelt out alreadie.

sp.speaker: NOTCH.
sp.p: Sir, we doe come from among the Brewhouſes in Saint Katherines, that's true, there you have ſmoak'd us (the Docke comfort your noſthrills,) and we may have lived in a miſt there, and ſo miſt our purpoſe; but for mine owne part I have brought my properties with me to expreſſe what I am; the keyes of my calling hang here at my girdle, and this the Regiſter booke of my function ſhewes mee no leſſe then a Clarke at all points, and a Brewers Clarke, and a Brewers head Clarke.

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: A man of accompt ſir! I cry you mercie.

sp.speaker: SLVG.
sp.p: I ſir, I knew him a fine Merchant, a merchant of Hops, till all hopt into the water.

sp.speaker: NOTCH.
sp.p:
No more of that, what I have beene, I have beene; what I am, I am: I Peter Notch, Clarke, hearing the Chriſtmas invention was drawne drie at Court; and that neither the KINGS Poet,
nor his Architect had wherewithall left to entertaine ſo much as a Baboone of quality, nor ſcarce the Welſh Embaſſadour if hee ſhould come there: Out of my allegiance, to wit, drew in ſome other friends that have as it were preſumed out of their own naturalls, to fill up the vacuum with ſome pretty preſentation, which we have addreſſed, and conveighed hither in a Lighter at the generall charge, and landed at the backe doore of the Buttery, through my neighbour Slug's credit there.

sp.speaker: SLVG.
sp.p: A poore Lighter-man ſir, one that hath had the honour ſometimes to lay in the Kings beere there; and I aſſure you I heard it in no worſe place then the very Buttry, for a certaine, there would bee no Maſque, and from ſuch as could command a jacke of beere, two, or three.

sp.speaker: VAN.
sp.p: Dat is all true, exceeding true, de inventors be barren, loſt, two, dre, vour mile, I know that from my ſelven; dey have no ting, no ting van deir owne, but dat dey take vrom de eard, or de zea, or de heaven, or de hell, or de reſt van de veir Clementen, de place a, dat be ſo common as de vench in de Burdello. Now me would bring in ſome dainty new ting, dat never was, nor never ſall be in de rebus natura; dat has neder van de materia, nor de forma, nor de hoffen, nor de voote, but a mera deviſa of de braine—

sp.speaker: GROOM.
sp.p: Hey-da! what Hans Flutter kin is this? what Dutchman doe's build or frame Caſtles in the Aire?

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p: He is no Dutch man ſir, he is a Brittaine borne, but hath learn'd to miſuſe his owne tongue in travell, and now ſpeakes all languages in ill Engliſh; a rare Artiſt he is ſir, and a Projector of Maſques. His Project in ours is, that we ſhould all come from the three dancing Beares in Saint Katherines (you may hap know it ſir) hard by where the Prieſt fell in, which Alehouſe is kept by a diſtreſſed Lady; whoſe name (for the honour of Knighthood) will not bee knowne; yet ſhe is come in perſon here Errant, to fill up the adventure with her two women that draw drinke under her, Gentlewomen borne all three, I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: SLVG.
sp.p: And were three of thoſe Gentlewomen that ſhould have acted in that famous matter of Englands joy in ſixe hundred and three.

sp.speaker: LADY.
sp.p: What talke you of England's joy, Gentlemen? you have another matter in hand I wis, Englands ſport and delight if you can manage it. The poore Cattle yonder are paſſing away the time, with a cheat loafe, and a bumbard of broken beere, how will ye diſpoſe of them?

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: Cattle! what cattle doe's ſhe meane?

sp.speaker: LADY.
sp.p: No worſe then the Kings game I aſſure you; The Beares, Beares both of qualitie and faſhion, right Beares, true Beares.

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p: A deviſe only to expreſſe the place from whence we come (my Ladies houſe) for which we have borrowed three very Beares that (as her Ladyſhip aforeſayd ſayes) are well bred, and can dance to preſent the ſigne, and the Beareward to ſtand for the ſigne-poaſt.

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: That is prettie; but are you ſure you have ſufficient Beares for the purpoſe.

sp.speaker: SLVG.
sp.p: Very ſufficient Beares as any are in the Ground, the Pariſh-Garden, and can dance at firſt ſight, and play their owne tunes if need bee. Iohn Vrſon the Beare-ward, offers to play them with any Citie-dancers chriſtned, for a ground meaſure.

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p:
Marry, for lofty tricks, or dancing on the Ropes hee will not
undertake, it is out of their element he ſayes. Sir, all our requeſt is ſince we are come, we may be admitted, if not for a Maſque, for an Antickmask; and as we ſhall deſerve therein, we deſire to be returned with credit to the Buttry from whence we came, for reward, or to the Porters Lodge with diſcredit, for our puniſhment.

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: To be whipt with your Beares? Well, I could bee willing to venture a good word in behalfe of the Game, if I were aſſured the aforeſayd game would be cleanly, and not fright the Ladies.

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p: For that ſir, the Bear-ward hath put in ſecuritie, by warranting my Ladie and her Women to dance the whole changes with them in ſafety; and for their abuſing the place you ſhall not need to feare, for he hath given them a kinde of Dyet-bread to binde them to their good behaviour.

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: Well, let them come; if you need one, Ile helpe you my ſelfe.

div.stage: Enter John Urſon with his Beares ſinging.

lg.l: THough it may ſeeme rude
For me to intrude,
With theſe my Beares by chance-a;
'Twere ſport for a King,
If they could ſing
As well as they can dance-a
Then to put you out
Of feare or doubt,
We came from St. Katharin-a;
Theſe dancing three,
By the helpe of mee,
Who am the Poſt of the ſigne-a
We ſell good ware,
And we need not care
Though Court, and Country knew it:
Our Ale's o' the beſt,
And each good gueſt
Prayes for their ſouls that brew it.
For any Ale-houſe,
We care not a lowſe,
Nor Taverne in all the Towne-a;
Nor the Vintry Cranes,
Nor St. Clements Danes,
Nor the Devill can put us down-a,
Who has once there beene,
Comes thither agen,
The liquour is ſo mighty;
Beere ſtrong and ſtale,
And ſo is our Ale,
And it burnes like Aquavita.
To a ſtranger there,
If any appeare,
Where never before he has bin;
We ſhew th' yron Gate,
The wheele of St. Kate,
And the place where the Prieſt fel in.
The Wives of Wapping
They trudge to our tapping,
And ſtill our Ale deſire;
And there ſit and drinke,
Till the ſpue, and ſtinke,
And often piſſe out our fire.
From morning to night,
And about to day-light,
They ſit and never grudge it;
Till the Fiſh-wives joyne
Their ſingle coyne,
And the Tinker pawnes his budget.
If their braines be not well,
Or their bladders doe ſwell,
To eaſe them of their burden;
My Ladie will come
With a bowle and a broome,
And her Hand-mayd with a Iorden.
From Court we invite
Lord, Ladie, and knight;
Squire, gentlman, yeoman and groom.
And all our ſtiffe drinkers,
Smiths, Porters, and Tinkers,
And the beggars ſhall give ye roome.

p.hi: How like you? how like you?

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: Excellent! The Beares have done learnedly, and ſweetly.

sp.speaker: VAN.
sp.p: Tis noting, tis noting; vill you ſee ſometing? Ick ſall bring in de Turk • chen, met all zin Baſhawes, and zin dirty towſand Yanitſaries met all zin Whooren Cunuken, all met an auder, de Sofie van Perſia, de Tartar Cham met de great King of Mogull, and make deir men, and deir horſe, and deir Elephant en be ſeene fight in de ayre, and be all killen, and aliven, and no ſuch ting. And all dis met de Ars van de Catropricks, by de refleſbie van de glaſſen.

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p: Oh, he is an admirable Artiſt.

sp.speaker: SLVG.
sp.p: And a halfe ſir.

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: But where will he place his glaſſes?

sp.speaker: VAN.
sp.p: Fow, dat is all ean, as it be two, dree, veir, vife touſand Mile off: Ick ſall multipliren de vizioun, met an ander ſecret dat Ick heb: Spreck, vat vil you haben?

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: Good ſir put him toot, bid him doe ſomething that is impoſſible; he will undertake it I warrant you.

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p: I doe not like the Mogul, nor the great Turke, nor the Tartar, their names are ſomewhat to big for the Roome; marry if he could ſhew us ſome Countrey Plaiers, ſtrolling about in ſeverall Shires, without licence from the Office, that would pleaſe I know whom, or ſome Welſh Pilgrims.

sp.speaker: VAN.
sp.p: Pilgrim? now yow talke of de Pilgrim, it come in my head, Ick vill ſhew yow all de whole brave Pilgrim o'de Vorld: de Pilgrim dat goe now, now at de inſtant, two, dre towſand Mile to de great Mahomet, at de Mecha, or here, dere, every where, make de fine Labyrints, and ſhew all de brave error in de vorld.

sp.speaker: SLVG.
sp.p: And ſhall we ſee it here?

p.hi: Yau, here, here, here in dis Roome, tis very Roome: vel vat is dat to yow if Ick doe de ting? vat an devill, vera boten devill?

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: Nay, good ſir be not angry.

sp.speaker: NOT.
sp.p: 'Tis a diſeaſe that followes all excellent men, they cannot governe their paſſions; but let him alone, try him one 'bout.

sp.speaker: GRO.
sp.p: I would try him, but what has all this to doe with our Maske?

sp.speaker: VAN.
sp.p: O Sir, all de better vor an Antick-maske, de more abſurd it be, and vrom de purpoſe, it be ever all de better. If it goe from de nature of de ting, it is de more Art: for deare is Art, and deare is Nature, yow ſall ſee. Hochos-pochos, Paucos, Palabros.

div.head: The Second Antimaske.
div.stage: Which was a perplex'd Dance of ſtraying and deform'd Pilgrims taking ſeverall pathes, till with the opening of the light above, and breaking forth of Apollo, they were all frighted away, and the Maine Maſque begun.

sp.speaker: APOLLO
sp.stage: Artes eximias quatuor Apollini acceptas tulit antiquitasdeſcending, Sung.
sp.l: IT is no dreame, you all doe wake, and ſee;
Behold, who comes!Sagittandi peretiam, unde apud Homerum, frequens illud Epithetom 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , longe jaculans. far-ſhooting Phoebus he
That can both hurt andMedicinam, unde Medici nomen adeptus. heale; and with hisMuſicam, unde 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , appellatus. voyce
Reare Townes, and make ſocieties rejoyce;
That taught the Muſes all their harmonie,

•••
〈…〉 , Qui ſalutari levat arte f • ſſos corporis artu • . And men the tunefull Art of Augurie.
Apollo ſtoopes, and when a God deſcends,
May Mortalls thinke he hath no vulgar ends.

stage.hi: Being neere the earth, he call'd theſe perſons following, who came forth as from their Tombes.

div.l:
Linus Appollinis & Terpſichores filius. Pauſ.LInus, and
Orpheus, Apollinis & Calliopes, de quibus Virg, in Ecloga inſcript. Non me Carminibus vincet, nec Thraetius Orpheus. Nec Linus, huic mater quamvis, atque hui • pater ad ••• Orphei Calliopea Lino formoſus Apollo. Orpheus,Branchus, Apollinis & Jances filius, de quo vid. Strab. lib. 4. & Statium, Thebaid. lib. 3—patrioque aequalis honori Branchus. Branchus, Jdmon, Apollinis & Aft • ries filius. De illo vid. Valer. Flac. lib. 1. Argonautic.— Contra Phoebius Idmon non pallore vtris non ullo honore comarum terriblis, plenus fatis, Phoeboque quieto cui genitor tribunt praenoſcere Divum Omina, ſeu Flammas, ſeu lubrica cominus exta ſeuplenum cert •• interroget • ëra penni • . Idmon, all

l.hi: My ſacred Sons, riſe at your Fathers call
From your immortall Graves; where ſleepe, not death,
Yet bindes your powers.
What ſacred breath
Doth re-inſpire us?

l.note: Phoemoen filia Phoebi quae prima carmen heroïcum cecinit. Heſiod. in Theog
l.hi: What heat creepes through me, as when burning ſteele
Is dipt in water?

sp.speaker: Apollo.

l.hi: I, Phoemonoe,

sp.l: Thy Father Phoebus's fury filleth thee;

l.hi: Confeſſe my Godhead; once againe I call,

sp.l: Let whole Apollo enter in you all,

l.hi: And follow me.
We flie, we doe not tread,
The Gods doe uſe to raviſh whom they lead.

div.stage: Apollo deſcended, ſhewed them where the King ſate, and ſung forward.
div.l: BEhold the love and care of all the Gods
Of the Ocean, and the happie Iles;
That whilſt the World about him is at ods,
Sits Crowned Lord here of himſelfe, and ſmiles.

sp.speaker: CHORVS.
sp.l: To ſee the erring mazes of mankinde;
Who ſeeke for that, doth puniſh them to finde.

div.stage: Then he advanced with them to the King.

sp.speaker: APOLLO.
sp.l: PRince of thy Peace, ſee what it is to love
The Powers above!
Jove hath commanded me
To viſit thee;

And in thine honour with myAlluſ ••• d illud Ovid • j Epiſtol. Epiſt. Parid. Ilion aſpi • ies, ſ • mata
que turribus altis Moenia Apol
•• ne e •• ruc •• a avore lyr ••
Muſique reare

Romulus urbe cona • ta, Collegium & Augures ••• inſtatuit, ipſe nobiles, ut apud Liu. Lib. & Tull. lib. 1. Optimus Augur. Eorum officium fuit auſpi
• ia captare & ex • i • s colligere ſigna futurarum rerum, Deorum
que moni • a conſiderare de eventibus proſperi • vel adverſis. Sacer erat Romanis & res regia habita, dig •• taſ
que penes patricios & principes viros manſit etiam apud • mperatores obtinuit unde ab Apolline noſtro, tales Praeſes pulchre deſignatus a Colledge here,
Of tunefull Augures, whoſe divining skill,
ſhall waite thee ſtill,
And be the Heralds of his higheſt will.
The worke is done,
And I have made their Preſident thy Sonne;
Great Mars too, on theſe nights,

Saltationes in rebus ſacris ad hibebantur apud omnes pene gentes: & à ſaliendo, ſeu ſaltatione ſacra ad ſaliare carmen inſtitut â • dlij dicti & Marti conſecrati. Omnes etiam qui ad cantum & tibiam ludebant Sal • j & Saliſubſul • dicebantur. Salius, 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 vet. gloſſ. & Pacuvi. Yond, yond afarre,

que eorum •• ſſent imperſi •• li. Temple are,
And each one guided by a ſtarre.

sp.speaker: CHORVS.
sp.l: Haſte, haſte, to meet them, and as they advance
'twixt every Dance;
Let us interpret their Prophetick trance.

div.stage: Here they fetch'd out the Maskers, and came before them with the Torch-bearers along the Stage, ſinging this full Song.

sp.speaker: APOLLO and CHORUS.
sp.l: WHich way, and whence the lightning flew,
Or how it burned, bright, and blew,
Deſigne, and figure by your lights:
Then forth, and ſhew the ſeverall flights

YourAugurandi ſcientia 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 dicta. Divinatio per aves. Aves aut Oſcines, aut Prepetes Oſcines, quae ore, Proepetes, quae volatu Augurium ſignificant▪ Pullitripudio. Aves auſpicatae, & Praepetes, Aquila, Vultur, Sanqualis ſeu oſſifraga, Triarches, ſive Buteo, Immuſſulus, Accipiter, Cygnus, Columba, Oſcines, Cornix, Cornus, Anſer, Ciconia, Ardea, Noctua, inauſpicatae; Milvus, • arra, Nycticorax, Striges, Hirundo, Picus, &c. Birds have made, or what the wing
Or voyce in Augurie doth bring.
Which hand the Crow cried on, how high
The Vulture, or the Erne did flie,
What wing the Swan made, and the Dove,
The Storke, and which did get above:
Shew all the Birds of food or Prey,
But paſſe by the unluckie Jay,
The Night-Crow, Swallow, or the Kite
Let thoſe have neither right, CHOR. Nor part,
In this nights art.

div.stage: The Torch-bearers daunced.
After which the Augures layd by their Staves, and Danced their Entrie, which done, APOLLO and the reſt, interpreted the Augurie.

sp.speaker: APOLLO.
sp.l:
THe Signes areHabebant dextra & laeva omnia; antica & poſtica; Orientalia & Occident • lia. Graeci cum ſe od Septentrionem obverterent, Ortum ad dextram habuere. Romani cum Meridiem in auſpicando cum tuerentur Ortum ad laevam habuere. Ita
que ſiniſtrae partes eadem ſunt Romanis quae Graecis dextrae ad ortum. Siniſtra igitur illis meliora, Dextra pejora: Graecis contrà. There hath not beene a voyce, or flight
Of ill Preſage. Linus. TheColumbae augura non niſi regibus dant; quia nunquam ſingulae volant: ſicut Rex nunquam ſelus incedit. Nuntiae pacis. bird that brings
Her Augurie alone to Kings
The Dove, hath flowne. Orpheus. And to thy peace
Fortunes and the Fates increaſe.

sp.speaker: BRANCHUS.
sp.l: Ardea, & Ardeola, rerum arduarum auſpicium. Minervae ſacra. Apud Homer. Ili • d. K. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Minerva's Hernſhaw and her Owle,
Doe both proclaime, thou ſhalt controle
The courſe of things. Idmon. As now they be
With tumult carried: Apollo. And live free
From hatred, faction, or the feare,
To blaſt the Olive thou doſt weare.

sp.speaker: CHORVS.
sp.l: More is behind, which theſe doe long to ſhow,
And what the Gods to ſo great vertue owe.

lg.l: Still, ſtill theAuſpicium, ab ave ſpecienda. Paul. Nam quod nos cum praepoſitione dicimus ASPICIO apud veteres ſine praepoſitione SPICIO dicebatur. Auſpice is ſo good,
We wiſh it were but underſtood;
It even puts Apollo
To all his ſtrengths of art, to follow,

Signa quae ſeſe offerent, erat multifaria: nam ſ • obieceretur avis aliqua, conſiderabatur quo volatu ferretur, an abliquo vel prono, vel ſupinomotu Corporis, quo flecteret, contorqueret, aut contraharet membra; qua in parte ſeoccultaret; an ad dextram vel ſiniſtraem canerent Oſcines, &c. The flights, and to devine
What's meant by every Signe.
Thou canſt not leſſe be, then the charge
of every Dietie.
That thus art left here to inlarge,
And ſhield their pietie!
Thy neighbours at thy fortune long have gaz'd,
But at thy wiſdome, all doe ſtand amaz'd.
And wiſh to be,
O'recome, or governed by thee!
Safetie it ſelfe ſo ſides thee, where thou goeſt,
And Fate ſtill offers what thou covet'ſt moſt!

div.stage: THE REVELLS.
After which Apollo went up to the King and Sung.
div.l: Doe not expect to heare of all
Your good at once, leſt it foreſtall
A ſweetneſſe would be new:
Some things the Fates would have conceal'd
From us the Gods, leſt being reveal'd
Our powers ſhall envy you.
It is enough your people learne
The reverence of your peace
As well as Strangers doe diſcerne
The Glories, by th'increaſe

And that theRomulus augur fuit, & Numa, & reliqui reges Romani ſicut ante eos Turnus, Rhamnetes & alij. Lacedemonij ſuis regibus Augurem Aſſeſſorem dabant, Cilices, Lycij, Cares, Arab • s, in ſumma veneratione habuerunt Auguria. princely Augur here, your Sonne
Doe by his Fathers lights his courſes run.

sp.speaker: CHORUS.
sp.l: Him ſhall you ſee triumphing over all
Both foes and vices: and your young and tall
Nephewes, his Sonnes grow up in your imbraces,
To give this Iland Princes in long races.

div.stage: Here the heaven opened; and Jove, with the Senate of the Gods, were diſcovered, while Apollo returne • to his Seat, and aſcending ſung.

sp.speaker: APOLLO.
sp.l: SEE heaven expecteth my returne▪
The forked fire begins to burne,
Jove beckons to me come.

sp.speaker: JOVE.
sp.l: Though Phoebus be the god of Arts,
Hee muſt not take on him all parts:
But leave his Frather ſome.

sp.speaker: APOLLO.
sp.l: My arts are only to obey. JOVE. Vide Orpheum in hymn. de omnip. Jovis. And mine to ſway
Jove is that one, whom firſt, midſt, laſt, you call
The power that governes, and conſerveth all;
Earth, Sea, and Ayre, are ſubject to our checke,
And Fate with heaven, moving at our beck.
Till Jove it ratifie,
It is no Augurie,
Though uttered by the mouth of Deſtinie.

sp.speaker: APOLLO.
sp.p: Deare father, give the Signe, and ſeale it then.

sp.speaker: The Earth riſeth.
sp.p: It is the ſuit of Earth and Men.

sp.speaker: JOVE.
sp.p: What doe their Mortals crave without our wrong?

sp.speaker: Earth with the reſt.
sp.l: That Jove will lend us this our Soveraigne long;
Let our grand-children, and not wee,
His want or Abſence ever ſee.

sp.speaker: JOVE.
sp.l: Your wiſh is bleſt.
Mos Jovis, annuendo votis & firmandis omnibus. Apud Homer, &c. Jove knocks his Chin againſt his breſt,
And firmes it with the reſt.

sp.speaker: CHORUS.
sp.l: Sing then his fame, through all the orbes; in even
Proportions, riſing ſtill, from Earth to Heaven:
And of the laſting of it leave to doubt,
The power of time ſhall never put that out.

div.p: This done, the whole Scaene ſhut, and the Maskers danced their laſt Dance.

div.head: TIME VINDICATED TO HIMSELFE, AND TO HIS HONORS.
In the preſentation at COVRT on Twelfth night. 1623.

q.l: — qui ſemirantur, in illos
Virus habe: nos haec novimus eſſe nihil.

div.head: TIME ƲINDICATED.
div.stage: A Trumpet ſounded.
FAME entreth, follow'd by the Curious, the Ey'd, the Ear'd, and the Nos'd.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: GIve eare, the worthy, heare what Fame proclaimes.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: What? what? I'ſt worth our eares?

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: Or eyes?

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: Or noſes?
For we are curious, Fame: indeed, the Curious.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: We come to ſpie.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: And hearken.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: And ſmell out.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: More than you underſtand, my hot Inquiſitors,

sp.speaker: NOES.
sp.p: We cannot tell.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: It may be.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: However, goe you on, let us alone.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: We may ſpie out, that, which you never mean't.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: And noſe the thing you ſent not. Firſt, whence come you?

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: I came from Saturne.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: Saturne, what is he?

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: Some Proteſtant I warrant you, a Time-ſerver,
As Fame her ſelfe is.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.l: You are neere the right.
Indeed, he is Time it ſelfe, and his name KRONOS,

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: How! Saturne! Chronos! and the Time it ſelfe!
You're found: inough. A notable old Pagan!

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: One of their Gods, and ea • es up his owne children.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: A Fencer, and do's travell with a ſith
Inſtead of a long-ſword.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.l: Hath beene oft call'd from it,
To be their Lord of miſrule.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.l: As Cincinnatus
Was from the plough, to be Dictator.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.l: Yes.
We need no interpreter, on, what of Time?

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.l: The Time hath ſent me with my Trumpe to ſummon
All ſorts of perſons worthy, to the view
Of ſome great ſpectacle he meanes to night,
T'exhibite; and with all ſolemnitie.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: O, we ſhall have his Saturnalia.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: His dayes of feaſt, and libertie agen.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: Where men might doe, and talke all that they liſt.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: Slaves of their lords.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: The ſervants of their maſters!

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: And ſubjects of their Soveraigne.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: Not ſo laviſh.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: It was a brave time that!

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.l: This will be better:
I ſpie it comming, peace. All the impoſtures,
The prodigies, diſeaſes, and diſtempers,
The knaveries of the Time, we ſhall ſee all now.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.l: And heare the paſſages, and ſeverall humors
Of men, as they are ſwayd by their affections:
Some grumbling, and ſome mutining, ſome ſcoffing,
Some pleas'd, ſome pyning, at all theſe we laughing.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: I have it here, here, ſtrong, the ſweat of it,
And the confuſion (which I love) I noſe it,
It tickles mee.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: My foure eies itch for it.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.l: And my eares tingle, would it would come forth:
This roome will not receive it.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: That's the feare.

div.stage: Enter CHRONO-MASTIX.

sp.speaker: CHRON.
sp.p: What? what? my friends, will not this roome receive?

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: That which the Time is preſently to ſhew us.

sp.speaker: CHRO.
sp.l: The Time? Lo I the man, that hate the time
That is, that love it not; and (though in ryme,
I here doe ſpeake it) with this whipp you ſee,
Doe laſh the Time, and am myſelfe laſh-free.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: Who's this?

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: 'Tis Chronomaſtix, the brave Satyre,

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: The gentleman-like Satyre, cares for no body,
His fore-head tip't with bayes, doe you not know him?

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: Yes Fame muſt know him, all the Town admires him.

sp.speaker: CHRO.
sp.l: If you would ſee Time quake and ſhake, but name us,
It is for that, we are both belov'd, and famous.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: We know, Sir. But the Time's now come about.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: And promiſeth all libertie.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: Nay licence.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: We ſhall doe what we liſt.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: Talke what we liſt.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: And cenſure whom we liſt, and how we liſt.

sp.speaker: CHRO.
sp.l: Then I will looke on Time, and love the ſame,
And drop my whip: who's this! my Miſtris! Fame!
The lady whom I honour, and adore!
What lucke had I not to ſee her before!
Pardon me, Madam, more than moſt accurſt,
That did not ſpie your Ladiſhip at firſt,
T'have giv'n the ſtoop, and to ſalute the skirts
Of her, to whom all Ladies elſe are flirts!
It is for you, I revell ſo in rime,
Deare Miſtris, not for hope I have the Time
Will grow the better by it. To ſerve Fame
Is all my end, and get my ſelfe a name.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.l: Away, I know thee not, wretched Impoſtor,
Creature of glory, Mountebanke of witte,
Selfe-loving Braggart, Fame doth ſound no trumpet
To ſuch vaine, empty fooles: 'Tis Infamy
Thou ſerv'ſt, and follow'ſt, ſcorne of all the Muſes,
Goe revell with thine ignorant admirers,
Let worthy names alone.

sp.speaker: CHRO.
sp.l: O, you the Curious,
Breath you to ſee a paſſage ſo injurious,
Done with deſpight, and carried with ſuch tumor
'Gainſt me, that am ſo much the friend of rumor?
(I would ſay Fame?) whoſe Muſe hath rid in rapture
On a ſoft ambling verſe to every capture,
From the ſtrong guard, to the weake childe that reades me,
And wonder both of him that loves, or dread's me!
Who with the laſh of my immortall pen
Have ſcourg'd all ſorts of vices, and of men!
Am I rewarded, thus? have I, I ſay,
From Envies ſelfe torne praiſe, and bayes away,
With which my glorious front, and word at large,
Triumphs in print at my admirers charge.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: Rare! how he talkes in verſe, juſt as he writes!

sp.speaker: CHRO.
sp.l: When have I walk't the ſtreets, but happy he
That had the finger firſt to point at mee,
Prentice, or Journeyman! The ſhop doth know it!
The unletter'd Clarke! major and minor Poet!
The Sempſter hath ſate ſtill as I paſs'd by,
And dropt her needle! Fiſh-wives ſtaid their cry▪
The Boy with buttons, and the Basket wench!
To vent their wares into my workes do trench!
A pudding-wife that would deſpiſe the Times,
Hath utter'd frequent pen'worths, through my rimes,
And, with them, div'd into the Chamber-maid,
And ſhe unto her Lady hath convay'd
The ſeaſon'd morſels, who hath ſent me penſions,
To cheriſh, and to heighten my inventions.
Well, Fame ſhall know it yet, I have my faction,
And friends about me, though it pleaſe detraction,
To doe me this affront. Come forth that love me,
And now, or never, ſpight of Fame, approve me.

div.stage: At this the Mutes come in.
THE ANTIMASQUERS.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: How now! what's here? Is hell broke looſe?

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.l: You'l ſee.
That he ha's favourers, Fame, and great ones too.
That unctuous Bounty, is the Boſſe of Belinſgate,

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: Who feaſts his Muſe with claret wine, and oyſters,

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: Growes big with Satyre;

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: Goes as long as an Elephant:

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: She labours, and lies in of his inventions,

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: Ha's a male-poem in her belly now,
Big as a colt,

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: That kicks at Time already,

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: And is no ſooner foald, but will neigh ſulphure:

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: The next?

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.l: A quondam Juſtice, that of late
Hath beene diſcarded out o'the pack o'the peace,
For ſome lewd levitie he holds in capite,
But conſtantly loves him. In dayes of yore,
He us'd to give the charge out of his poems,
He carries him about him, in his pocket,
As Philip's Sonne did Homer, in a casket,
And cries, O happy Man, to the wrong party,
Meaning the Poet, where he meant the ſubject:

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: What are this paire?

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: The ragged raſcalls?

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.l: Meere rogues, you'ld thinke them rogues, but they are friends,
One is his Printer in diſguiſe, and keepes
His preſſe in a hollow tree, where to conceale him,
He workes by glow-worme light, the Moone's too open.
The other zealous ragge is the Compoſitor,
Who in an angle, where the ants inhabite,
(The emblem's of his labours) will ſit curl'd
Whole dayes, and nights, and worke his eyes out for him.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: Strange arguments of love! There is a Schoolemaſter
Is turning all his workes too, into Latine,
To pure Satyricke Latine; makes his Boyes
To learne him; calls him the times Juvenal;
Hangs all his Schoole with his ſharpe ſentences;
And o're the Execution place hath painted
Time whipt, for terror to the Infantery.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.l: This Man of warre, i'the rere, He is both Trumpet
And Champion to his Muſe.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: For the whole City.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: H'as him by roat, recites him at the tables,
Where he doth governe; ſweares him into name,
Upon his word, and ſword, for the ſole youth
Dares make profeſſion of Poetick truth,
Now militant amongſt us: To th'incredulous,
That dagger is an article he uſes,
To rivet his reſpect into their pates,
And make them faithful. Fame, you'l find you'ave wrongd him.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: What a confederacie of Folly is here!

div.stage: They all daunce but Fame, and make the firſt Antimaſque, In which they adore, and carry forth the Satyre, and the Curious come up agen.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: Now Fame, how like you this?

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.l: This falls upon you
For your neglect.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: He ſcornes you, and defies you,
H'as got a Fame on's owne, as well as a Faction.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: And theſe will deifie him, to deſpite you.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.l: I envie not the 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 .
'Twill prove but deifying of a Pompion.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: Well, what is that the Time will now exhibite?

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: What gambols? what deviſes? what new ſports?

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: You promis'd us, we ſhould have any thing.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: That Time would give us all we could imagine.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: You might imagine ſo, I never promis'd it.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.l: Pox, then 'tis nothing. I had now a fancie
We might have talk'd o'the King.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: Or State.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: Or all the World.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: Cenſur'd the Counſell, e're they cenſure us.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: We doe it in Pauls.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: Yes, and in all the tavernes!

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.l: A comely licence. They that cenſure thoſe
They ought to reverence, meet they that old curſe,
To beg their bread, and feele eternall Winter.
Ther's difference 'twixt liberty, and licence.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: Why if it be not that, let it be this then
(For ſince you grant us freedome, we will hold it,)
Let's have the giddy world turn'd the heeles upward,
And ſing a rare blacke Sanctus, on his head,
Of all things out of order.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.l: No, the Man
I'the Moone daunce a Corranto, his buſh
At's backe, a fire; and his dogge piping Lachrimae.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.l: Or let's have all the people in an uprore,
None knowing, why, or to what end: and in
The midd'ſt of all, ſtart up an old mad woman
Preaching of patience.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: No, no, I'ld ha' this.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: Any thing.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.l: That could be monſtrous:
Enough, I meane. A Babel of wild humours.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: And all diſputing of all things they know not,

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: And talking of all men they never heard of,

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: And all together by the eares o'the ſudden,

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.l: And, when the matter is at hotteſt, then
All fall aſleepe.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.l: Agree among your ſelves,
And what it is you'ld have, I'le anſwer you.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: O, that we ſhall never doe.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: No, never agree.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: Not upon what. Something that is unlawfull.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: I, or unreaſonable.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: Or impoſſible.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: Let 't be uncivill enough, you hit us right.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: And a great noyſe.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: To little, or no purpoſe.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: And if there be ſome miſchiefe, 'twill become it.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: But ſee, there be no cauſe, as you will anſwer it.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: Theſe are meere Monſters.

sp.speaker: NOSE.
sp.p: I, all the better.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.l: You doe abuſe the Time. Theſe are fit freedomes
For lawleſſe Prentices, on a Shrovetueſday,
When they compell the Time to ſerve their riot.
For drunken Wakes, and ſtrutting Beare-baytings,
That ſavour only of their owne abuſes.

sp.speaker: EIES.
sp.p: Why, if not thoſe, then ſomething to make ſport.

sp.speaker: EARES.
sp.p: Wee only hunt for novelty, not truth.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.p: I'le fit you, though the Time faintly permit it.

div.stage: The ſecond Antimaſque of Tamblers, and Juglers, brought in by the Cat and fiddle, who make ſport with the Curious, and drive them away.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.l: Why now they are kindly us'd, like ſuch ſpectators,
That know not what they would have. Commonly,
The curious are ill natur'd, and like flies,
Seeke Times corrupted parts to blow upon:
But may the ſound ones live with fame, and honour,
Free from the moleſtation of theſe Inſects:
Who being fled, Fame now perſues her errand.

div.stage: Loud MVSIQUE.
To which the whole Scene opens, where Saturne ſitting with Venus is diſcover'd above, and certaine Votaries comming forth below, which are the Chorus.

sp.speaker: FAME.
sp.l: For you, great King, to whom the Time doth owe
All his reſpects, and reverence, behold
How Saturne, urged at requeſt of Love,
Prepares the object to the place to night.
Within yond' darkneſſe, Venus hath found out
That Hecate (as ſhe is Queene of ſhades)
Keepes certaine glories of the Time obſcur'd,
There, for her ſelfe alone to gaze upon,
As ſhe did once the faire Endimion.
Theſe, Time hath promis'd at Loves ſuit to free,
As being fitter to adorne the age,
By you reſtor'd on earth, moſt like his owne:
And fill this world of beautie here, your Court.
To which his bountie, ſee, how men prepare
To fit their votes below, and thronging come
With longing paſſion to enjoy th'effect!
Harke, it is Love begins to Time. Expect.

sp.speaker: VENUS.
sp.l: Beſide, that it is done for Love,
It is a worke, great Time, will prove
Thy honour, as mens hopes above.

sp.speaker: SATURNE.
sp.l: If Love be pleaſed, ſo am I:
For Time could never yet deny
What Love did aske, if Love knew why.

sp.speaker: VOTARIES.
sp.l: Shee knew, and hath expreſt it now.
And ſo doth every publike vow
That heard her why, and waites thy how.

sp.speaker: SATURNE.
sp.l: You ſhall not long expect: with eaſe
The things come forth, are borne to pleaſs:
Looke, have you ſeene ſuch lights as theſe?

div.stage: The Maſquers are diſcovered, and that which obſcur'd them, vaniſheth.

sp.speaker: VOTARIES.
sp.p: Theſe, theſe muſt ſure ſome wonders bee!

sp.speaker: CHORUS.
sp.l: O, what a glory 'tis to ſee
Mens wiſhes, Time, and Love agree

div.stage: {A Pauſe
There SATVRNE and VENVS paſſe away, and the Maſquers deſcend.

sp.speaker: CHORUS.
sp.l: What griefe, or envie had it beene,
That theſe, and ſuch had not beene ſeene,
But ſtill obſcur'd in ſhade!
Who are the glories of the Time,
Of youth, and feature too, the prime,
And for the light were made!

sp.speaker: VOTARIES.
sp.l: 1 Their very number, how it takes!
2 What harmony their preſence makes!
3 How they inflame the place!

sp.speaker: CHORVS.
sp.l: Now they are neerer ſeene, and viewd;
For whom could Love have better ſu'd?
Or Time have done the grace?

div.stage: Hereto a loud Muſique, they march into their figure. and daunce their ENTRY, or firſt DAVNCE.
After which.

sp.speaker: VENUS.
sp.l: The night could not theſe glories miſſe,
Good Time, I hope, is ta'ne with this.

sp.speaker: SATURNE.
sp.l: If Time were not, I'am ſure Love is.
Betweene us it ſhall be no ſtrife:
For now 'tis Love, gives Time his life.

sp.speaker: VOTARIES.
sp.l: Let Time then ſo with Love conſpire,
as ſtraight be ſent into the court
A little Cupid, arm'd with fire,
Attended by a jocund Sport,
To breed delight, and a deſire
of being delighted, in the nobler ſort.

sp.speaker: SATURNE.
sp.p: The wiſh is crown'd, as ſoone as made.

sp.speaker: VOTARIES.
sp.l: And CVPID conquers, e're he doth invade.
His victories of lighteſt trouble prove.
For there is never labour, where is Love.

div.stage: Then, followes the maine DAVNCE, which done, CVPID, with the SPORT, goes out.

sp.speaker: CUPID.
sp.l: Take breath awhile, young Blouds, to bring
Your forces up, whilſt we goe ſing
Freſh charges, to the Beauties here.

sp.speaker: SPORT.
sp.l: Or, if they charge you, doe not feare,
Though they be better arm'd then you:
It is but ſtanding the firſt view,
And then they yeeld.

sp.speaker: CUPID.
sp.p: Or quit the field.

sp.speaker: SPORT.
sp.l: Nay, that they'l never doe.
They'l rather fall upon the place,
Then ſuffer ſuch diſgrace.
You are but Men at beſt, they ſay,
And they from thoſe ne're ran away.

div.stage: {Pauſe.

sp.speaker: CUIPID.
sp.l: You, Sir, that are the Lord of Time,
Receive it not as any crime
'Gainſt Majeſty, that Love and Sport
Tonight have entred in your Court.

sp.speaker: SPORT.
sp.l: Sir, doubt him more of ſome ſurpriſe
Vpon your ſelfe. He hath his eyes.
You are the nobleſt object here,
And 'tis for you alone I feare:
For here are Ladyes, that would give
A brave reward, to make Love live
Well, all his life, for ſuch a draught.
And therefore, looke to every ſhaft,
The Wags a Deacon in his craft.

div.stage: {Pauſe.

sp.speaker: CUPID.
sp.l: My Lords, the Honors of the Crowne,
Put off your ſowreneſſe, doe not frown • ,
Bid cares depart, and buſineſſe hence:
A little, for the Time diſpence.

sp.speaker: SPORT.
sp.l: Truſt nothing that the Boy lets fall,
My Lords, he hath plots upon you all.
A Penſioner unto your wives,
To keepe you inuxorious gives,
And ſo your ſenſe to faſcinate,
To make you quit all thought of ſtate,
His amorous queſtions to debate.
But, heare his Logicke, he will prove
There is no buſineſſe, but to be in love.

sp.speaker: CUPID.
sp.l: The words of Sport, my Lords, and courſe.
Your Ladyes yet, will not thinke worſe
Of Love for this: they ſhall command
My Bow, my Quiver, and my Hand.

sp.speaker: SPORT.
sp.l: What, here to ſtand
and kill the Flies?
Alas, thy ſervice they deſpiſe.
One Beauty here, hath in her eyes,
More ſhafts then from thy bow o're flew,
Or that poore quiver knew.
Theſe Dames,
They need not Love's, they have Natures flames:

sp.speaker: CUPID.
sp.p: I ſee the Beauty, that you ſo report.

sp.speaker: SPORT.
sp.l: Cupid, you muſt not point in Court;
Where live ſo many of a ſort.
Of Harmony theſe learn'd their ſpeech,
The Graces did them footing teach,
And, at the old Idalian bralls,
They daunc'd your Mother downe. Shee calls.

sp.speaker: CUPID.
sp.p: Arme, arme then all.

sp.speaker: SPORT.
sp.l: Young blouds come on,
And charge: Let every man take one.

sp.speaker: CUPID.
sp.p: And try his fate.

sp.speaker: SPORT.
sp.l: Theſe are faire warres.
And will be carried without ſcarres.

sp.speaker: CUPID.
sp.l: A joyning, but of feet, and hands.
Is all the Time, and Love commands.

sp.speaker: SPORT.
sp.l: Or if you doe their gloves off-ſtrip.
Or taſte the Nectar of the lip:
See, ſo you temper your deſires,
For kiſſes, that yee ſucke not fires.

div.stage: The REVELS follow, which ended, the CHORVS appeare agen, and DIANA deſcends to HIPPOLITUS, the whole Scene being chang'd to a Wood, out of which he comes.

sp.speaker: CHORUS.
sp.l: The Courtly ſtrife is done, it ſhould appeare,
Betweene the Youths, and Beauties of the yeare,
Wee hope that now theſe lights will know their ſpheare,
And ſtrive hereafter to ſhine ever here:
Like brighteſt Planets, ſtill to move
In th'eye of Time, and orbes of Love.

sp.speaker: DIANA.
sp.l: Hippolitus, Hippolitus.

sp.speaker: HIPPOLITUS.
sp.l: Diana?

sp.speaker: DIANA.
sp.l: Shee.
Be ready you, or Cephalus,
To waite on me.

sp.speaker: HIPPOLITUS.
sp.l: Wee ever be.

sp.speaker: DIANA.
sp.l: Your Goddeſſe hath beene wrong'd to night,
By Loves report unto the Time.

sp.speaker: HIPPOLITUS.
sp.l: The injury, it ſelfe will right,
Which only Fame hath made a crime.
For Time is wiſe,
And hath his eares as perfect as his eyes.

sp.speaker: SATURNE.
sp.l: Who's that deſcends? Diana?

sp.speaker: VOTARIES.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: VENUS.
sp.l: By like her troope ſhee hath begun to miſſe.

sp.speaker: SATURNE.
sp.l: Let's meet, and queſtion what her errand is.

sp.speaker: HIPPOLITVS.
sp.l: Shee will prevent thee, Saturne, not t' ••• uſ •
Her-ſelfe unto thee, rather to complaine
That thou and Venus both ſhould ſo abuſe
The name of Dian, as to entertaine
A thought, that ſhe had purpoſe to defraud
The Time, of any glories that nere his:
To doe Time honour rather, and applaud
His worth, hath beene her ſtudy.

sp.speaker: DIANA.
sp.l: And it is.
I call'd theſe Youth's forth; in their bloud; and prime
(Out of the honour, th •• I bore their parts)
To make them fitter ſo to ſerve the Time
By labour, riding, and thoſe ancient arts,
That firſt enabled men unto the warres,
And furniſh'd Heaven with ſo many Starres:

sp.speaker: HIPPOLITVS.
sp.l: As Perſeus, Caſtor, Pollux, and the reſt,
Who were of Hunters firſt, of Men the beſt;
Whoſe ſhades doe yet remaine within yond' groves,
Themſelves there ſporting with their nobler loves:

sp.speaker: DIANA.
sp.p: And ſo may theſe doe, if the Time give leave.

sp.speaker: SATURNE.
sp.l: Chaſt Dians purpoſe we doe now conceive,
And yeeld thereto.

sp.speaker: VENVS.
sp.p: And ſo doth Love.

sp.speaker: VOTARIES.
sp.p: All Votes doe in one circle move.

sp.speaker: CHORVS.
sp.l: Turne Hunters then,
agen.
Hunting, it is the nobleſt exerciſe,
Makes men laborious, active, wiſe,
Brings health, and doth the ſpirits delight,
It help's the hearing, and the ſight:
It teacheth arts that never ſlip
The memory, good horſmanſhip,
Search, ſharpneſſe, courage, and defence,
And chaſeth all ill habits thence.
Turne Hunters then,
agen,
But not of men.
Follow his ample;
And juſt example,
That hates all chace of malice, and of bloud:
And ſtudies only wayes of good,
To keepe ſoft Peace in breath.
Man ſhould not hunt Mankind to death,
But ſtrike the enemies of Man;
Kill vices if you can:
They are your wildeſt beaſts.
And when they thickeſt fall, you make the Gods true feaſts.

div.head: NEPTUNES TRIUMPH FOR THE RETVRNE OF ALBION.
CELEBRATED IN A Maſque At the Court on the Twelfth night. 1624.

q.p: Omnis & ad reducem jam litat ara Deum.

div.head: NEPTVNES TRIVMPH.
div.stage: HIs Matie being ſet, and the loude Muſique ceaſing. All, that is diſcovered of a Scene, are two erected Pillars, dedicated to Neptune, with this inſcription upon the one, NEP. RED. On the other, SEC. IOV.
The POET entring on the STAGE, to diſperſe the Argument, is call'd to by the Maſter-Cooke.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: Doe you heare, you, Creature of diligence, and buſineſſe! what is the affaire, that you plucke for ſo, under your cloake?

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: Nothing, but what I colour for, I aſſure you; and may encounter with, I hope, if Luck favour me, the Gamſters Goddeſſe.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: You are a Votary of hers, it ſeemes by your language. What went you upon? may a man aske you?

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: Certainties, indeed Sir, and very good ones; the preſentation of a Maſque; you'll ſee't, anone.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: Sir, this is my roome, and region too, the banquetting-houſe. And in matter of feaſt, the ſolemnitie, nothing is to be preſented here, but with my acquaintance, and allowance to it.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: You are not his Majeſties Confectioner? Are you?

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: No, but one that has as good title to the roome, his Maſter-Cooke. What are you, Sir?

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: The moſt unprofitable of his ſervants, I, Sir, the Poet. A kind of a Chriſtmas Ingine? one, that is uſed, at leaſt once a yeare, for a trifling inſtrument, of wit, or ſo.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: Were you ever a Cooke?

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: A Cooke? no ſurely.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: Then you can be no good Poet: for a good Poet differs nothing at all from a Maſter-Cooke. Eithers Art is the wiſedome of the Mind.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: As how, Sir?

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: Expect. I am by my place, to know how to pleaſe the palates of the gueſts; ſo, you, are to know the palate of the times: ſtudy the ſeverall taſtes, what every Nation, the Spaniard, the Dutch, the French, the Walloun, the Neapolitan, the Brittan, the Sicilian, can expect from you.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: That were a heavie and hard taske, to ſatisfie Expectation, who is ſo ſevere an exactreſſe of duties; ever a tyrannous miſtreſſe: and moſt times a preſſing enemie.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: She is a powerfull great Lady, Sir, at all times, and muſt be ſatisfied: So muſt her ſiſter, Madam Curioſitie, who hath as daintie a palate as ſhe, and theſe will expect.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: But, what if they expect more then they underſtand?

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p:
That's all one, Mr. Poet. you are bound to ſatisfie them. For, there is a palate of the Underſtanding, as well as of the Senſes. The Taſte is taken with good reliſhes, the Sight with faire objects, the Hearing with delicate ſounds, the Smelling with pure ſents, the feeling with ſoft and plumpe bodyes, but the Underſtanding with all theſe: for all which you muſt begin at the Kitchin. There, the Art of Poetrie was learn'd,
and found out, or no where: and the ſame day, with the Art of Cookery.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: I ſhould have giv'n it rather to the Cellar, if my ſuffrage had bin askt.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: O, you are for the Oracle of the Bottle, I ſee; Hogſhead Triſmegiſtus: He is your Pegaſus. Thence flowes the ſpring of your Muſes, from that hoofe.
sp.l: Seduced Poet, I doe ſay to thee,—
A Boyler, Range, and Dreſſer were the fountaines
Of all the knowledge, in the Univerſe,
And that's the Kitchin. Where, a Maſter-Cooke!
Thou do'ſt not know the man! nor canſt thou know him!
Till thou haſt ſerv'd ſome yeares in that deepe ſchoole,
That's both the Nource, and Mother of the Arts,
And hear'ſt him read, interpret, and demonſtrate.
A Maſter-Cooke! why, he is the man of men,
For a Profeſſor! He deſignes, he drawes,
He paints, he carves, he builds, he fortifies,
Makes Citadels of curious fowle, and fiſh,
Some he dry-ditches, ſome motes round with broths;
Mounts marrow-bones; cuts fifty-angled cuſtards;
Reares bulwarke pies; and, for his outer workes,
He raiſeth ramparts of immortall cruſt;
And teacheth all the tacticks at one dinner:
What rankes, what files, to put his diſhes in
The whole Art Militarie! Then he knowes
The influence of the ſtarres, upon his meates;
And all their ſeaſons, tempers, qualities,
And ſo, to fit his reliſhes, and ſauces!
He, has Nature in a pot! 'bove all the Chemiſts,
Or bare-breech'd brethren of the Roſie-Croſſe!
He is an Architect, an Inginer,
A Souldier, a Phyſition, a Philoſopher,
A generall Mathematician!

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: It is granted.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: And, that you may not doubt him for a Poet,

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: This Fury ſhewes, if there were nothing elſe.
And 'tis divine!

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: Then, Brother Poet,

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: Brother.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: I have a ſuite.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: What is it?

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: Your deviſe.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: As you came in upon me, I was then
Offering the argument, and this it is.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: Silence.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: The mightie Neptune, mightie in his ſtyles,
And large command of waters, and of Iſles,
Not, as the Lord and Soveraigne of the Seas,
But, Chiefe in the art of riding, late did pleaſe
To ſend his Albion forth, the moſt his owne,
Upon diſcovery, to themſelves beſt knowne,
Through Celtiberia; and, to aſſiſt his courſe,
Gave him his powerfull MANAGER of Horſe,
With divine Proteus, Father of diſguiſe,
To waite upon them with his counſels wiſe,
In all extreames. His great commands being done,
And he deſirous to review his Sonne,
He doth diſpatch a floting Ile, from hence,
Unto the Heſperian ſhores, to waft him thence.
Where, what the arts were, us'd to make him ſtay,
And how the Syrens woo'd him, by the way,
What Monſters he encountred on the coaſt,
How neere our generall Joy was to be loſt,
Is not our ſubject now: though all theſe make
The preſent gladneſſe greater, for their ſake.
But what the triumphs are, the feaſt, the ſport,
And proud ſolemnities of Neptunes Court,
Now he is ſafe, and Fame's not heard in vaine,
But we behold our happie pledge againe.
That with him, loyall HIPPIVS is return'd,
Who for it, under ſo much envie, burn'd
With his owne brightneſſe, till her ſterv'd ſnakes ſaw
What Neptune did impoſe, to him was law.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: But, why not this, till now?

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: —It was not time,
To mixe this Muſick with the vulgars chime.
Stay, till th'abortive, and extemporall dinne
Of balladry, were underſtood a ſinne,
Minerva cry'd: that, what tumultuous verſe,
Or proſe could make, or ſteale, they might rehearſe,
And every Songſter had ſung out his fit;
That all the Countrey, and the Citie-wit,
Of bells, and bonfires, and good cheere was ſpent,
And Neptunes Guard had drunke all that they meant;
That all the tales and ſtories now were old
Of the Sea-Monſter Archy, or growne cold:
The Muſes then might venter, undeterr'd,
For they love, then, to ſing, when they are heard.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: I like it well, 'tis handſome: and I have
Some thing would fit this. How doe you preſent 'hem?
In a fine Iland, ſay you?

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: Yes, a Delus:
Such, as when faire Latona fell in travaile,
Great Neptune made emergent.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: I conceive you.
I would have had your Ile brought floting in, now
In a brave broth, and of a ſprightly greene,
Juſt to the colour of the Sea; and then,
Some twentie Syrens, ſinging in the kettel,
With an Arion, mounted on the backe
Of a growne Conger, but in ſuch a poſture,
As, all the world ſhould take him for a Dolphin:
O, 'twould ha'made ſuch muſick! Ha'you nothing,
But a bare Iſland?

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: Yes, we have a tree too,
Which we doe call the Tree of Harmonie,
And is the ſame with what we read, the Sunne,
Brought forth in the Indian Muſicana firſt,
And thus it growes. The goodly bole, being got
To certaine cubits height, from every ſide
The boughes decline, which taking roote afreſh,
Spring up new boles, and thoſe ſpring new, and newer,
Till the whole tree become a Porticus,
Or arched Arbour, able to receive
A numerous troupe, ſuch as our Albion,
And the Companions of his journey are.
And this they ſit in.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: Your prime Maſquers?

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: But where's your Antimaſque now, all this while?
I hearken after them.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: Faith, we have none.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: None?

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: None, I aſſure you, neither doe I thinke them
A worthy part of preſentation,
Being things ſo heterogene, to all deviſe,
Meere By-workes, and at beſt Out-landiſh nothings.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: O, you are all the heaven awrie! Sir.
For blood of Poetry, running in your veines,
Make not your ſelfe ſo ignorantly ſimple.
Becauſe Sir, you ſhall ſee I am a Poet,
No leſſe then Cooke, and that I find you want
A ſpeciall ſervice here, an Antimaſque,
I'le fit you with a diſh out of the Kitchin,
Such, as I thinke, will take the preſent palates,
A metaphoricall diſh! And, doe but marke,
How a good wit may jumpe with you. Are you ready, Child?
(Had there bin Maske, or no Maske, I had made it.)
Child of the boyling houſe.

sp.speaker: CHILD.
sp.p: Here, Father.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: Bring forth the pot. It is an Olla Podrida,
But I have perſons, to preſent the meates.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: Perſons!

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: Such as doe reliſh nothing, but di ſtato,
(But in another faſhion, then you dreame of)
Know all things the wrong way, talke of the affaires,
The clouds, the cortines, and the myſteries
That are a foot, and, from what hands they have'hem
(The maſter of the Elephant, or the Camels)
What correſpondences are held; the Poſts
That goe, and come, and know, almoſt, their minutes,
All but their buſineſſe: Therein, they are fiſhes.
But ha' their garlick, as the Proverb ſayes,
They are our Queſt of enquiry, after newes.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: Together with their learned Authors?

sp.speaker: CHILD.
sp.l: Yes Sir,
And of the Epicoene gender, Hees, and Shees:
Amphibion Archy is the chiefe.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: Good boy!
The Child is learned too. Note but the Kitchin.
Have you put him, into the pot, for Garlick?

sp.speaker: CHILD.
sp.l: One in his coate, ſhall ſtinke as ſtrong as he, Sir,
And his friend Giblets with him.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: They are two,
That give a part of the ſeaſoning.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: I coneeive
The way of your Gally-mawfrey.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: You will like it,
When they come pouring out of the pot together.

sp.speaker: CHILD.
sp.p: O, if the pot had beene big enough!

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: What then, Child?

sp.speaker: CHILD.
sp.p: I had put in the Elephant, and one Camel, at leaſt, for Biefe.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: But, whom ha'you for Partridge?

sp.speaker: CHILD.
sp.p: A brace of Dwarfes, and delicate plump birds!

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: And whom for Mutton, and Kid?

sp.speaker: CHILD.
sp.l: A fine lac'd Mutton,
Or two; and either has her frisking Husband:
That reades her the Corranto, every weeke.
Grave Mr. Ambler, Newes-maſter of Poules,
Supplies your Capon; and growne Captaine BuZ
(His Emiſſary) under-writes for Turky,
A gentleman of the Forreſt preſents Pheſant,
And a plump Poultrers wife, in Graces ſtreet,
Playes Hen with egges i' the belly, or a Coney,
Chooſe which you will.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: But, where's the Bacon, Thom?

sp.speaker: CHILD.
sp.l: Hogrel the Butcher, and the Sow his wife,
Are both there.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: It is well, goe, diſh'hem out.
Are they well boyld?

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: What's that? rotten?

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: O, that they muſt be. There's one maine ingredient
We have forgot, the Artichoke.

sp.speaker: CHILD.
sp.l: No Sir.
I have a Fruicterer, with a cold red noſe,
Like a blue fig, performes it.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.l: The fruit lookes ſo.
Good child, goe poure'hem out; ſhew their concoction.
They muſt be rotten boyld, the broth's the beſt on't,
And that's the Dance. The ſtage here is the Charger.
And Brother Poet, though the ſerious part
Be yours, yet, envie not the Cooke his art.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: Not I. Nam luſus ipſe Triumphus amat.

div.stage: The Antimaſque is danc'd by the perſons deſcrib'd, comming out of the pot.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.p: Well, now, expect the Scene it ſelfe; it opens!

div.stage: The Iland is diſcovered, the Masquers ſitting in their ſeverall ſieges. The heavens opening, and Apollo, with Mercury, ſome Muſes, & the Goddeſſe Harmony, make the muſique, the while, the Iland moves forward, Proteus ſitting below, and APOLLO ſings.

sp.speaker: APOLLO.
sp.l: Looke forth, the Shepherd of the Seas,
And of the Ports, that keep'ſt the keyes,
And to your Neptune tell,
His ALBION, Prince of all his Iſles,
For whom the ſea, and land ſo ſmiles,
Is home returned well.

lg.l: And be it thought no common Cauſe,
That, to it, ſo much wonder drawes,
And all the Heav'ns conſent,
With HARMONY, to tune their notes,
In anſwer to the publike votes,
That, for it, up were ſent.
It was no envious Stepdames rage;
Or Tyrants malice of the age,
That did employ him forth.
But ſuch a Wiſdome, that would prove,
By ſending him, their hearts, and love
That elſe might feare his worth.

div.stage: By this time, the Iſland hath joyned it ſelfe with the ſhore: And Proteus, Portunus, and Saron; come forth, and goe up ſinging to the State, while the Maſquers take time to Land.

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.l: I! now the Pompe of Neptunes triumph ſhines!
And all the glories of his great deſignes
Are read, reflected, in his ſonnes returne!

sp.speaker: PORTVNVS.
sp.l: How all the eyes, the lookes, the heart here burne
at his arrivall!

sp.speaker: SARON.
sp.l: Theſe are the true fires.
Are made of joyes!

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.p: Of longing!

sp.speaker: PORTVNVS.
sp.p: Of deſires!

sp.speaker: SARON.
sp.p: Of hopes!

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.p: Of feares!

sp.speaker: PORTVNVS.
sp.p: No intermitted blocks.

sp.speaker: SARON.
sp.p: But pure affections, and from odorous ſtocks!

sp.speaker: CHORVS.
sp.l: 'Tis incenſe all, that flames!
And theſe materials ſcarce have names!

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.l: My King lookes higher, as he ſcorn'd the warres
Of windes, and with his trident touch'd the ſtarres.
There is no wrinkle in his brow, or frowne;
But, as his cares he would in Nectar drowne,
And all the ſilver-footed Nymphs were dreſt;
To waite upon him, to the Oceans feaſt.

sp.speaker: PORTVNVS.
sp.l: Or, here in rowes upon the bankes were ſet,
And had their ſeverall hayres made into net
To catch the youths in, as they come on ſhore.

sp.speaker: SARON.
sp.l: How! Galatea ſighing! O, no more.
Baniſh your feares.

sp.speaker: PORTVNVS.
sp.l: And Doris dry your teares.
Albion is come:

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.l: And Haliclyon, too,
That kept his ſide, as he was charg'd to doe,
With wonder.

sp.speaker: SARON.
sp.p: —And the Syrens have him not.

sp.speaker: PORTVNVS.
sp.l: Though they no practiſe, nor no arts forgot,
That might have wonne him, or by charme, or ſong.

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.l: Or laying forth their treſſes all along
Upon the glaſsie waves;

sp.speaker: PORTVNVS.
sp.p: Then diving:

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.l: Then,
Up with their heads, as they were mad of men.

sp.speaker: SARON.
sp.l: And there, the higheſt-going billowes crowne,
Untill ſome luſtie Sea-god pull'd them downe.

sp.speaker: CHORVS.
sp.p: See! He is here!

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.l: Great Maſter of the mayne,
Receive thy deare, and precious pawne againe.

sp.speaker: CHORVS.
sp.l: SARON, PORTVNVS, PROTEVS, bring him thus,
Safe, as thy Subjects wiſhes gave him us:
And of thy glorious Triumph let it be
No leſſe a part, that thou their loves doeſt ſee,
Then, that his ſacred head's return'd to thee.

div.stage: This ſung, the Iſland goes backe, whilſt the upper Chorus takes it from them, and the Maſquers prepare for their figure.

sp.speaker: CHORVS.
sp.l: Spring all the Graces of the age,
And all the Loves of time;
Bring all the pleaſures of the ſtage,
And reliſhes of rime:
Adde all the ſoftneſſes of Courts
The lookes, the laughters, and the ſports.
And mingle all their ſweets, and ſalts,
That none may ſay, the Triumph halts.

div.stage: Here, the Maſquers daunce their Entry.
Which done, the firſt proſpective of a maritime Palace, or the houſe of Oceanus is diſcovered, with lowd Muſique.
And the other above is no more ſeene.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: Behold the Palace of Oceanus!
Hayle Reverend ſtructure! Boaſt no more to us
Thy being able, all the Gods to feaſts;
We have ſeene enough: our Albion was thy gueſt.

div.stage: Then followes the Maine Daunce. After which the ſecond proſpect of the Sea, is ſhowne, to the former Muſicke.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: Now turne and view the wonders of the deepe,
Where Proteus herds, and Neptunes Orkes doe keepe,
Where all is plough'd, yet ſtill the paſture's greene
The wayes are found; and yet no pathes are ſeene.

div.stage: There Proteus, Portunus, Saron, goe up to the Ladyes with this Song,

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.l: Come noble Nymphs, and doe not hide
The joyes, for which you ſo provide:

sp.speaker: SARON.
sp.l: If not to mingle with the men,
What doe you here? goe home agen.

sp.speaker: PORTVNVS.
sp.l: Your dreſsing doe confeſſe,
By what we ſee, ſo curious parts
Of Pallas, and Arachnes arts,
That you could meane no leſſe.

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.l: Why doe you weare the Silke-wormes toyles;
Or glory in the ſhell-fiſh ſpoyles?
Or ſtrive to ſhew the graines of ore
That you have gather'd on the ſhore,
Whereof to make a ſtocke
To graft the greener Emerald on
Or any better-water'd ſtone?

sp.speaker: SARON.
sp.p: Or Ruby of the rocke?

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.l: Why doe you ſmell of Amber gris,
Of which was formed Neptunes Neice,
The Queene of Love; unleſſe you can
Like Sea-borne Venus love a man?

sp.speaker: SARON.
sp.p: Try, put your ſelves unto't.

sp.speaker: CHORVS.
sp.l: Your lookes, your ſmiles, and thoughts that meet,
Ambroſian hands, and ſilver feet,
doe promiſe you will do't.

div.stage: The Revells follow. Which ended, the Fleete is diſcovered, while the three Cornets play.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: 'Tis time, your eyes ſhould be refreſh'd at length
With ſomething new, a part of Neptunes ſtrength
See, yond', his fleete, ready to goe, or come,
Or fetch the riches of the Ocean home,
So to ſecure him both in peace, and warres,
Till not one ſhip alone, but all be ſtarres.

div.stage: A ſhout within followes. After which the Cooke enters.

sp.speaker: COOKE.
sp.p: I have another ſervice for you, Brother Poet, a diſh of pickled Saylors, fine ſalt Sea-boyes, ſhall reliſh like Anchoves, or Caveare, to draw downe a cup of Nectar, in the skirts of a night.

sp.speaker: SAYLORS.
sp.p: Come away boyes, the Towne is ours, hay for Neptune, and our young Maſter.

sp.speaker: POET.
sp.l: He knowes the Compaſſe, and the Card,
While Caſtor ſits on the maine yard,
And Pollux too, to helpe your hayles;
And bright Leucothoe, fils your ſayles:
Arion ſings, the Dolphins ſwim,
And, all the way, to gaze on him.

div.stage: The Antimaſque of Saylors. Then The laſt Song to the whole Muſique, five Lutes, three Cornets, and ten voyces.

sp.speaker: PROTEVS.
sp.l: Although we wiſh the Triumph ſtill might laſt
For ſuch a Prince, and his diſcovery paſt,
Yet now, great Lord of waters, and of Iſles,
Give Proteus leave to turne unto his wiles:

sp.speaker: PORTVNVS.
sp.l: And, whilſt young Albion doth thy labours • aſe,
Diſpatch Portunus to thy Ports,

sp.speaker: SARON.
sp.l: And Saron to thy Seas:
To meet old Nereus, with his fifty girles,
From aged Indus laden home with Pearles,
And orient gummes, to burne unto thy name.

sp.speaker: CHORVS.
sp.l: And may thy Subjects hearts be all on flame:
Whilſt thou doſt keepe the earth in firme eſtate,
And 'mongſt the winds doſt ſuffer no debate.
But both at Sea, and Land, our powers increaſe
With health, and all the golden gifts of peace.

div.stage: The laſt Daunce.

div.head: PANS ANNIVERSARIE; OR, THE SHEPHERDS HOLY-DAY.
THE SCENE ARCADIA. As it was preſented at Court before King JAMES. 1625.
div.p: The Inventors, Inigo Iones. Ben. Iohnſon.
div.stage: The firſt preſentation is of three Nymphs ſtrewing ſeverall ſorts o • flowers, followed by an old Shepherd with a Cenſer and perfumes.

l.hi: THus, thus, begin the yearly rites
Are due to PAN on theſe bright nights;
His Morne now riſeth, and invites
To ſports, to dances, and delights:
All Envious, and Prophane away,
This is the Shepherds Holy-day.
Strew, ſtrew, the glad and ſmiling ground
With every flower, yet not confound
The Prime-roſe drop, the Springs owne ſpouſe,
Bright Dayes-eyes, and the lips of Cowes,
The Garden-ſtar, the Queene of May,
The Roſe, to crowne the Holy-day.
Drop, drop you Violets, change your hues,
Now red, now pale, as Lovers uſe,
And in your death goe out as well,
As when you liv'd unto the ſmell:
That from your odour all may ſay,
This is the Shepherds Holy-day.

sp.speaker: SHEPHERD.

l.hi: Well done my pretty ones, raine Roſes ſtill,
Untill the laſt be drapt: Then hence: and-fill
Your fragrant prickles for a ſecond ſhower,

sp.l: Bring Corn-flag, Tulips, and Adonis flower,

l.hi: Faire Oxe-eye, Goldy-locks, and Columbine,
Pinkes, Goulands, King-cups, and ſweet Sops-in-wine,
Blew Harebells, Pagles, Panſies, Calaminth,
Flower-gentle, and the faire-hair'd Hyacinth,
Bring rich Carnations, Floure-de-luces, Lillies,
The chequ'd, and purple-ringed Daffodillies,
Bright Crowne-imperiall, Kings-ſpeare, Holy-hocks,

sp.l: Sweet Venus Navill, and ſoft Lady-ſmocks,
Bring too, ſome branches forth of Daphnes haire,

l.hi: And gladdeſt myrtle for theſe poſtes to weare
With Spikenard weav'd, and Marjoram betweene,
And ſtar'd with yellow-golds, and Meadowes • ueene,
That when the Altar, as it ought is dreſt,
More odour come not from the Phaenix neſt;

sp.l: The breadth thereof Panchaia may envie,
The colours China, and the light the skye.

div.stage: LOUD MUSIQUE.
The Scene opens, and in it are the Maſquers diſcover'd ſitting about the Fountaine of light.
The Muſicians attyr'd like the Prieſts of Pan ſtanding in the worke beneath them, when entreth to the old Shepherd.

sp.speaker: A Fencer flouriſhing.
sp.p: Roome for an old Trophie of Time; a Sonne of the ſword, a Servant of Mars, the Minion of the Muſes, and a Maſter of Fence. One that hath ſhowne his quarters, and plaid his prizes at all the games of Greece in his time; as Fencing, Wreſtling, Leaping, Dauncing, what not? And hath now uſher'd hither by the light of my long-ſword certaine bold Boyes of Baeotia, who are come to challenge the Arcadians at their owne ſports, call them forth on their owne holy-day, and Daunce them down on their owne Greene-ſwarth.

sp.speaker: SHEPHERD.
sp.p: 'Tis boldly attempted, and muſt be a Baeotian enterpriſe by the face of it, from all the parts of Greece elſe, eſpecially at this time when the beſt, and braveſt ſpirits of Arcadia, called together by the excellent Arcas, are yonder ſitting about the Fountaine of light, in conſultation of what honours they may doe the great Pan by encreaſe of anniverſarie rites fitted to the Muſique of his peace.

sp.speaker: FENCER.
sp.p: Peace to thy Pan, and mum to thy Muſique, Swaine; There is a Tinker of Thebes a comming, called Epam, with his kettle will make all Arcadia ring of him; What are your ſports for the purpoſe? ſay, if ſinging, you ſhall be ſung downe, if dauncing, daunc'd downe. There is no more to be done with you, but know what; which it is; and you are in ſmoke, gone, vapour'd, vaniſh'd, blowne, and (as a man would ſay) in a word of two ſillables, Nothing.

sp.speaker: SHEPHERD.
sp.p: This is ſhort, though not ſo ſweet. Surely the better part of the ſolemnitie here will be dauncing.

sp.speaker: FENCER.
sp.p: Enough; They ſhall be met with inſtantly in their owne ſphere, the ſphere of their owne activitie a daunce. But by whom, expect: No Cynaetheian, nor Satyres; but (as I ſaid) Boyes of Baeotia; thinges of Thebes, (the Towne is ours, Shepheard) mad merry Greekes, Lads of life, that have no gall in us, but all ayre and ſweetneſſe. A Tooth-drawer is our Foreman, that if there be but a bitter tooth in the company, it may bee called out at a twitch; he doth command any mans teeth out of his head upon the point of his Poynard; or tickles them forth with his ryding rod: Hee drawes teeth a horſe-backe in full ſpeed, yet hee will daunce a foot, he hath given his word: He is yeoman of the mouth to the whole Brotherhood, and is charged to ſee their gummes bee cleane, and their breath ſweet, at a minutes warning. Then comes my learned Theban, the Tinker I told you of, with his kettle Drum (before and after) a Maſter of Muſique, and a man of mettall; He beates the march to the tune of Tickle-foot, Pam, pam, pam, brave Epam with a nondas. That's the ſtraine.

sp.speaker: SHEPHERD.
sp.p: A high one.

sp.speaker: FENCER.
sp.p: Which is followed by the trace, and tract of an excellent Juggler, that can juggle with every joynt about him, from head to heele. He can doe tricks with his toes, wind ſilke, and thred Pearle with them, as nimble a fine fellow of his feet, as his hands: For there is a noble Corne-cutter his companion, hath ſo pared, and finified them—. Indeed, he hath taken it into his care, to reforme the feet of all, and fit all their footing to a forme; onely ones play-foot in the company, and he is a Bellowes-mender, allow'd who hath the looking to of all their lungs by patent, and by his place is to ſet that leg afore ſtill, and with his puffes keepes them in breath during pleaſure; A Tinder-box-man to ſtrike new fire into them at every turne, and where he ſpies any brave ſparke that is in danger to goe out, plie him with a match preſently.

sp.speaker: SHEPHERD.
sp.p: A moſt politique proviſion.

sp.speaker: FENCER.
sp.p:
Nay, we have made our proviſions beyond example, I hope. For to theſe there is annexed a Clock-keeper, a grave perſon, as Time himſelfe, who is to ſee that they all keepe time to a nick, and move every elbow in order, every knee in compaſſe. He is to wind them up, and draw them downe as he ſees cauſe; Then is there a ſubtile ſhrewd-bearded Sir, that
